p01.text: On March 12 the first statement of the new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, aired on state television. There was no voice of his own. An announcer read it for him. The statement said the Strait of Hormuz would stay closed and warned countries hosting U.S. bases. The same day the U.N. refugee agency said the war had driven three million people from their homes inside Iran.

p02.text: The same day fire broke out in the laundry spaces of the carrier USS Gerald R. Ford in the Red Sea. Two sailors were hurt and more than 600 lost their bunks. Fighting it and cleaning up took thirty hours. In western Iraq a U.S. Air Force KC-135 tanker crashed, killing all six crew. Ten Iranian multiple-warhead missiles fell on Tel Aviv, injuring 124.

p03.text: On March 13 U.S. forces bombed Kharg Island, the hub of Iran’s crude exports. President Trump said every military facility on the island had been destroyed. In Tehran an explosion during the Quds Day march killed one person. The State Department posted rewards of up to $10 million on ten Iranian leaders, Mojtaba Khamenei among them.

p04.text: On March 14 President Trump called on Britain, France, China, South Korea, Japan and others to send warships to the Strait of Hormuz. The same day the Indian tankers Shivalik and Nanda Devi slipped safely through the strait after talks between the Indian and Iranian foreign ministers. A fire broke out at the UAE’s Fujairah oil terminal. A road opened by bombs and a road opened by a phone call lay side by side.

p05.text: On March 15 the Revolutionary Guards said they had fired their 50th wave of attacks at U.S. bases in the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait. Joint U.S.-Israeli strikes killed fifteen people in Isfahan. A human rights group logged 494 airstrikes that day alone. In Lebanon 886 people had been killed in two weeks. The war was fought in the sky. Its weight piled up on the ground.

p06.text: The new leader did not come as a voice. He came through someone else’s mouth. Dr. Leila Shirazi watched Iranian state TV. An anchor in black read from a sheet of paper. On screen there was one old photograph: the son, half hidden behind his father. One thing was different from the father’s speeches. There were no pauses for the crowd to shout. Writing done in a bunker. “Is he even alive?” Sam asked.

p07.text: “A living man wrote it. Who wrote it is another question.” On the right-hand screen Fordow kept the same pulse it had kept for twelve days. The statement had the strait in it. Nothing nuclear. On her desk, a figure: three million. Was her aunt Fereshte one of them? Her aunt was not a woman who left her roses. The numbers count the people who leave. Not the ones who stay.

p08.text: The enemy did not come as a missile. It came up a dryer exhaust duct. Capt. Marcus Webb went down to Damage Control Central. On a hundred-thousand-ton ship, fire is an older enemy than missiles. The men on the hoses were cooks, deckhands, yeomen. Kids who had launched aircraft eighteen hours a day for thirteen days were putting out the fire in their own bunks.

p09.text: When it was out he walked the burned compartments. Bunk frames melted together. A family photo, half burned, stuck to the deck. He pulled his hand back; it would crumble. “Six hundred with nowhere to sleep, Captain.” “Put cots in the hangar bay. Give them my cabin too. Write the families first, starting with: everybody’s alive.” Today his hands were not still. They had soot on them and shook a little. Strangely, that was a relief.

p10.text: It was the last Friday of Ramadan. Quds Day. Soraya Tahir leaned on a closed bookstore’s shutter and watched the avenue. Flags. Pictures of the dead leader. She tried to hate the march. It belonged to the system that had locked her up in 2022. But she could see faces. A woman pushing a stroller. An old man on a cane. Where bombs fall, belief and fear and anger clot into one lump.

p11.text: An explosion in the distance. The march faltered, then walked on. The slogans got louder. Those people were raising their voices in front of something frightening, too. Only the songs were different. “The firewood?” “In the basement. Four days to go.” Slogans on the avenue, the spring song hiding in the alleys. Bombing does not make a country one. It only pushes two countries under one roof.

p12.text: Sarah Callahan sat in the bathtub of a windowless bathroom, writing her story. The satellite phone rang. The second mate of a tanker anchored deep in the Gulf. From Kerala, India, twenty-nine. “The northern horizon’s red. That’s toward Kharg.” “What do you have left on board?” “Eleven days of water. Vegetables ran out. That’s not the problem. We’re sitting on two million barrels of oil, ma’am.”

p13.text: “Every night you hear drones. Every time one goes over, twenty-three men stop breathing. Every day I write my mother a text. I can’t send it.” Sarah took out her notebook. “People write that the strait is blocked. We are not blocked. We are forgotten. Please write it that way.” On the map of a war only the warships are drawn. The ships between them, on nobody’s side, are not.

p14.text: The cable from Seoul was one line. Report on-scene assessment. Lt. Kim Junho knew what it was asking. The American president had told South Korea, too, to send warships. He stood at the whiteboard. On the left, the ships hit near the strait in two weeks. On the right, the two Indian ships that went through yesterday. The strait was not closed. It had a doorman. Ships from countries that could talk to Tehran got through.

p15.text: He wrote the report. First paragraph, facts. Second, the Indian case. In the third his hand stopped. But his father had said a soldier who loses the strength to think is no soldier. A warship can escort a ship. It cannot bring out a ship already trapped. He read it three times and sent it. His hands shook. The first time he had put his own name behind an opinion.

p16.text: Nariman was seven. The sun drawn on the glass had long since been wiped away. For the first time in sixteen days Maryam had a day off. Last night: nine hours, two transfusions, one amputation. “Maman, when is Baba coming?” Her husband, Davood, was a Revolutionary Guards sergeant. One phone call twelve days ago was the last. The child had been asleep. Every day Maryam regretted not waking her. “Soon.”

p17.text: At seven you don’t know yet when soon is. Two days of milk left in the fridge. No allergy medicine at the pharmacy. The pharmacist said next week. Next week was one kind of soon too. “Maman, when the war’s over, can we have ice cream?” “Of course. The biggest one. The three of us, with Baba.” She should not have said the last part. Nariman held up three fingers. That promise was Maryam’s now.

p18.text: Col. Darius Sepahvand read the damage tally three times. Two search radars left. Eleven usable interceptors. The commander who took over the post above him died within days, and so did the next one. An army where the higher you went, the shorter you lived. Yesterday he had talked to his daughter Narges for forty seconds. He told her to get out. “I’m not going. Who’ll carry water up for the old lady downstairs?”

p19.text: “Father, who are you guarding right now? Us, or them?” He could not answer. Guarding the sky meant not asking whom you guarded. In the winter of 2020, the day his own country’s missile brought down an airliner, that simplicity cracked. Now his daughter had split it in two. He sent up his report. Radars: 2. Interceptors: 11. What he wanted to write, he could not write yet.

p20.text: Sunday, four in the afternoon, the hour he would have taught. The university had stopped classes on the third day of the war. Professor Azad Moradi came anyway. Sixty empty chairs. Last semester’s chalk was still on the board: panta rhei, everything flows. He began to lecture to the empty chairs. “Can a just man live in an unjust state? That is today’s subject.”

p21.text: “Socrates drank the hemlock. But the dialogues remained.” On the board he wrote: logos menei, the word remains. From the doorway the custodian asked, “Will you teach next week too?” “I will.” That evening in Seoul, Kang Yujin sat before a model that had missed two Indian ships. It knew warships and missiles. Not phone calls between foreign ministers. She added one variable. Negotiation.
